lines.note: Wakiganna names a kind of carpenter's plane, matching maneira de cepilho. The middle of Hua is worn; no secure nasal mark is supplied merely because Hũa would be familiar elsewhere.
Wakigakebukuro is a bag carried at the side. Alforge and saco introduce the Portuguese description, whose users are identified on the following two physical rows.

runs.text: vſão os pobres que andão pedindo, ou outras

lines.note: The bag is used by poor people who go begging, or by other people. The small rounded final letter supports vſão, correcting OCR vſãr while preserving the printed historical form.
Peßoas completes outras peßoas, extending the bag's use beyond beggars. This short continuation is a complete physical row, not part of the next entry.
Wakige is armpit hair, directly explained by cabelos do souaco. The narrow i before gue is damaged but visible; Vaqigue corrects the OCR Vaqague and its misleading generated reading.

runs.text: Vaqijde, zzuru, eta. i, Vaqide, uru.

lines.note: Wakiide and wakide are the paired verbs here; the principal forms zzuru and eta belong to the first form. Vide directs the reader to the earlier entry rather than adding a new gloss.
Suprà completes the direction to look above for wakide. The grave accent is retained, and this short Latin continuation remains separate from the following verb.
Wakii, wakiiru, wakiitta describes water settling after boiling. The Portuguese infinitive aquietarse begins the explanation, and fer- continues as ferueo on the next row.

runs.text: ueo, ou deixar de ſoar a feruura. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Ferueo completes the description of water that has boiled; the alternative is the sound of boiling ceasing. The pilcrow then introduces another sense on the following line.

runs.text: Minguar a agoa com a feruura.

lines.note: The additional sense is water diminishing through boiling. Minguar refers to loss of volume, distinct from the quieting described in the preceding definition.
Wakimaye means understanding or distinguishing, as the paired Portuguese verbs explain. The following example applies discernment to one's awareness or composure.

Iengouo vaqimayenu is zengo wo wakimaenu, failing to discern what is before and after oneself; the Portuguese renders it as lacking awareness. The scan supports n and the initial I type, correcting leugouo; the omitted pilcrow is restored.

runs.text: do de ſi ¶ Item, Pagar o fiador pollo acrè-

lines.note: Do completes acordo, so the first gloss is not having one's wits about one. The entry then turns to payment by a guarantor; the printed phrase pollo acrè- is retained without silently repairing its debtor-creditor terminology.

runs.text: dor, ou recompenſar outro o que hum não po-

lines.note: Dor completes acrèdor, followed by compensation to another for what someone cannot pay. The row continues the financial sense of wakimaye, rather than the initial intellectual sense.

runs.text: de pagar. ¶ Item aliquindo, Pagar as di

lines.note: De finishes pode; the next clause concerns paying debts of one's own. The visible aliquindo is retained as an anomalous or damaged form understood as Latin aliquando, 'sometimes', rather than silently regularized. The unhyphenated di continues into uidas below.

runs.text: uidas proprias, ſed non tam propriè.

lines.note: Uidas completes diuidas, and proprias specifies one's own debts. The Latin qualification sed non tam propriè says this usage is less proper; it is retained as part of the printed explanation.

The gloss identifies a shortcut or secret path, corresponding to wakimichi. The scan prints the contiguous anomalous Vaqinichi with a single n; NINJAL's Vaqimichi is only a lexical aid and does not authorize replacing that letter. The locally italic initial V is retained. Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, v202510, CC BY 4.0, https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html.

Wakinoo and waki no noo are alternative forms referred back to Vaqi. The circumflexes are visible; Vide and the referenced Japanese term form a cross-reference rather than a standalone example sentence.

runs.text: Fedor, ou ruim cheiro dos ſouacos.

lines.note: Waki no ka means the smell of the armpits. Portuguese fedor and ruim cheiro emphasize an unpleasant smell, distinct from the hair entry above.
Waki no ita denotes armour protecting the flanks or sides. Armas is used in the protective-equipment sense established by ilhargas and lados.
Wakitachi gives the onset or vigorous rising of a boil. The principal forms tçu and atta are preserved, while the Portuguese agoa is divided as a- and goa across the physical rows.
Goa completes agoa; feruer em burbulhões explains boiling in large bubbles. This continuation belongs to wakitachi and retains the printed Portuguese spelling.
Wakitame is redirected to wakimaye as the preferred word. The cross-referenced principal form continues onto the next line; no independent definition is supplied here.
Uru completes the cross-reference to Vaqimaye, uru. Que he propria palaura identifies it as the proper expression, explaining why the preceding entry points elsewhere.
Wakitsubo is the hollow beneath the arm or the armpit. The Portuguese gives both the physical location and the ordinary body-part name.
Wakite has the adverbial meaning particularly or especially. The short gloss is complete on this row and does not depend on the following wakivaki entry.
Wakiwaki refers to people of lesser rank or standing. Inferiores and gente somenos define a social category rather than the anatomical meaning of waki.
Wakiwakini means privately or among the lesser people. Emparticular is retained as the printed joined form, and the ensuing example illustrates unofficial talk.

Wakiwakini yuuta koto wo hon ni itasu-na warns against treating what was privately said as authoritative. The negative particle na is divided onto the next row; the printed long-u mark and fonni spelling are retained.

runs.text: Não façais caſo do que ſe diz pellos cã-

lines.note: Na completes the prohibition. The Portuguese says not to attach importance to what is said in corners; cã- begins cantos across the physical break.

runs.text: tos, ou o que dizem os particulares que não ſão

lines.note: Tos completes cantos, followed by what private people say who are not superiors. The centre of particulares is abraded, but the surviving strokes and sentence support it over OCR partinulares; this local damage remains a reading caveat.
Superiores completes the contrast between private talk and statements by those in authority. The visible ending supports ſuperiores rather than OCR ſuperiares.
Wakisendoo is an officer immediately subordinate to a ship's commander. The small mark over the final o points upward: Vaqixendô corrects the OCR caron without changing the word's letters.

runs.text: ao capitão, ou ao mestre, ou dono do nauio.

lines.note: The officer is next below the captain, master, or owner of the vessel. These Portuguese alternatives complete the rank description rather than introducing three Japanese headwords.
Wakizashi is glossed simply as a dagger. The historical Portuguese category adaga is retained without substituting a modern classification of Japanese swords.
Wakoo is explained by hikari wo yawaraguru, softening light or radiance. Vaquǒ has a visible caron, contrasting with the circumflex in the nearby ship-officer entry.

Temperar o resplandor completes the explanation of moderating radiance. Wakoo doojin then names the religious expression whose Portuguese explanation follows; its two different long-vowel marks are preserved.

runs.text: Diz ſe dos Camis que vierão a este mundo mo-

lines.note: The explanation concerns kami who came into this world while moderating their manifestation. Camis is a Japanese-derived term embedded in Portuguese prose; the line ends with mo-, beginning modificando.

Dificando completes modificando, describing the moderation of their light and majesty, followed by mixing themselves with human beings. The final misturã- preserves its abbreviation mark and printed division.

runs.text: doſe com noſco que ſomos ciſco.

lines.note: Dose completes misturãdose; com nosco que somos cisco characterizes humans as dust or refuse. This concludes the explanation of wakoo doojin, including its figurative contrast.
Wara is straw. The brief standalone gloss prepares the material common to the following footwear and mat entries but remains an independent dictionary entry.
Warabakimono is straw footwear compared with alparcas. The scan shows a capital Ç in Çapatos and contiguous alpar- at the line end, correcting OCR Capatos and the spurious internal space.

Cas completes alparcas; in the Cami region the footwear is called Varacongǒ. Both Cami and the quoted alternative occur inside a Portuguese regional explanation, rather than as an independent Japanese sentence.
Warabe means a child, here given as minino. The historical Portuguese vowel is retained instead of modernizing the gloss to menino.
Warabi is described as edible herbs or greens. The entry's broad gloss is retained without adding a botanical species identification that this line does not print.
Warakongoo sends the reader back to warabakimono. The caron is visible, and Vide marks a cross-reference to the straw-footwear entry already explained above.

Waraji is followed by the preferred form Varanzzu and the start of a straw-shoe definition. The scan supports italic Meliùs, two z letters in Varanzzu, and Certos rather than OCR Centos; the definition continues at the top of column 2.

zones.label: Column 2 running header
zones.note: The running header visibly prints ATES without an N or a secure nasal abbreviation; this is retained rather than normalized to ANTES.

runs.text: de palha como alparcas que ſe atão nos pès.

lines.note: Completes the preceding column's Certos çapatos: straw footwear like alparcas, tied onto the feet. The column transition is continuous body text, and the visible grave accent in pès is retained.
Waragutsu is given the same meaning as the straw footwear just described. Idem supplies the complete gloss, with no omitted continuation before the following verb.
Warai gives the verb for laughing and its printed principal forms; dotto waroo illustrates a sudden collective laugh. The three long-o marks are carons in the scan and are preserved individually.
The Portuguese explains many people laughing loudly together. A new example begins hito wo wa-, with the verb continued onto the next physical line.
Rǒ completes hito wo waroo, laughing at or mocking somebody. Zombar and rir dalguem explain the directed, derisive use rather than general laughter.
The noun warai first means laughter and then mockery. Zõ- is the printed first part of zombaria; its nasal abbreviation and line-end mark are retained.
Baria completes zombaria. Banmin no warai to naru means becoming the object of everyone's laughter; the Portuguese translation begins with ser on this row.

runs.text: eſcarneo do pouo, ou de todos.

lines.note: Escarneo do pouo, ou de todos completes the translation as becoming a public laughingstock. It belongs to the preceding example rather than constituting another sense of the next verb.
Waraiai describes people laughing together or at one another, with the yǒ and yǒta principal forms shown. The scan's Rirenſe is retained rather than regularized to a modern Portuguese spelling.
Ou entre si adds the reciprocal interpretation, among themselves. This short continuation completes the collective-laughing verb and stays separate from the next face-related noun.
Waraigao and emigao name a smiling face. Rosto riſonho supplies the facial expression; the provisional st rendering is retained under the project's separate ligature-audit policy.
E alegre completes the description of the smiling face as cheerful. It remains an independent physical row despite the brevity of the continuation.
Waraigoto is a ridiculous or laughable matter. The example begins waraigo- and continues into the phrase for becoming a subject of mockery on the next line.

runs.text: Ser, ou ficar por couſa de zõbaria.

lines.note: Toni naru completes waraigoto ni naru. The Portuguese explains becoming, or ending up as, an object of mockery, preserving the printed zõbaria abbreviation.

runs.text: Couſa de riſo, ou occaſião de riſo.

lines.note: Waraigusa is something that provokes laughter or an occasion for laughter. The long s in the Japanese form is retained as printed rather than converted to the modern spelling's s.
Waraigusa ni naru means becoming material for laughter. The pilcrow visible before the example was absent from the OCR and has been restored; the Portuguese explanation continues below.
De riso e zombaria completes materia, making the person or thing a subject of laughter and mockery. This completes the example begun on the preceding physical row.
Waraitate is glossed as many people laughing together. The historical principal form tçuru is retained, and the alternative action is completed on the following line.
Ou zombarem dalguem adds mocking someone as the alternative gloss. It closes the laughing verb before the new straw-mat headword.
Waramushiro is a straw mat, directly matched by esteira de palha. The scan reads Varamuxiro without the extra i introduced by OCR Varamuixiro.
Waranbe is another child term, again glossed minino. The n before b is retained as part of this printed form rather than assimilated to the nearby Varabe spelling.
Warawa is the first-person expression identified here as used by women. The note records the dictionary's own usage description without projecting a modern register onto it.
Waraya is a straw house or a house covered with straw. The Portuguese says only casa de palha, so no more specific construction method is supplied.

Warazzu and waraji are presented as alternatives, followed by a direction to the earlier Varagi entry. Vide corrects OCR Tide; the first varagi is a Japanese synonym, whereas the final Varagi is the Portuguese cross-reference's target.
Ware first means I, then less properly thou or you. The Latin minùs propriè qualifies the second-person use, whose social circumstances are stated below.

runs.text: falando com gente baixa, ou abatendo a alguem.

lines.note: The second-person use addresses people of low status or belittles the addressee. This completes the usage qualification for ware rather than defining a new pronoun.

runs.text: Vare, uru, eta. De Vari, u.

lines.note: Ware, waruru, wareta is related to the transitive Vari, u; take ga waruru illustrates bamboo splitting. De is visibly upright here, while Vt is italic; the printed typefaces are preserved rather than assigned by language alone.

Fẽderse a cana translates the bamboo splitting; the visible mark above e abbreviates the nasal and corrects OCR Federſe. The following example begins tsubo, chawan ga waru-, concerning vessels that break.
Ru completes the intransitive verb. The Portuguese specifies a jar or porcelain vessel breaking, retaining the historical forms boyão and porſolana.

Ita, or ji, with ga hiwaruru describes a board or the ground cracking of itself. Fivaruru is the visible historical verb form and is not silently reduced to varuru; abrirse por si introduces the translation.

runs.text: ou fender a taboa, abrir aterra, &c. fender

lines.note: The translation mentions splitting a board and opening the ground, then repeats the general splitting sense. The printed &c. separates those examples from the general restatement; fender continues into se below without an invented hyphen.
Se completes fenderse and is paired with quebrarse. Per met. introduces the figurative example kuni ga wa-, whose verb is continued on the next row.

runs.text: Auer algũas guerras, & brigas no rei

lines.note: Ruru completes kuni ga waruru, a country becoming divided. The gloss begins wars and quarrels in the kingdom; rei continues as reino below without a printed line-end hyphen.
No completes reino and locates those disputes among nobles. A further example begins uchiwa ga waru-, describing division within an associated group.

runs.text: Auer diſcordias, ou bandos entre os par

lines.note: Ru completes the example; discordias and bandos describe disagreements or factions. Par continues into particulares on the next physical row, with no supplied terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ticulares que ſão ſubditos dalgum ſenhor, ou eſ-

lines.note: Ticulares completes particulares, the people who are subjects of a lord. The alternative clause begins eſ-, completed as eſtão on the following row.

runs.text: tão de baixo de hũa meſma milicia.

lines.note: Tão completes eſtão; the people belong under the same military organization. This closes the extended figurative account of a group splitting into factions.

runs.text: Pedaço de couſa que ſe quebra. ¶

lines.note: The noun ware is a piece broken from something. The comparison with kake begins as Ca- and continues on the following physical row.

runs.text: Pedacinho mais pequeno como da bor-

lines.note: Qe completes kake, defined as a smaller fragment such as a piece of an edge. Bor- begins borda, and the comparison distinguishes the size or character of the broken piece.
Da completes borda, followed by et cetera. This short row finishes the fragment comparison and is not furniture or part of the following bamboo entry.
Waredake is split or cleft bamboo. The voiced d of this form is preserved separately from the Varetaqe variant printed several rows below.

runs.text: Hũa roſa, ou fula que nace de hũa

lines.note: Waremokoo is described by its flower, called a rose or fula growing from an herb. The unusual but visible fula is retained without changing it to flor; the plant description continues on the next line.
Erua completes the plant description, and Item, Ameſma erua extends the name to the herb itself. The punctuation after Item is a comma, correcting the OCR full stop.
Warera is glossed as either we or I. This preserves the dictionary's allowance for plural and singular reference rather than forcing the modern plural interpretation.
Waretake is again split or cleft bamboo. The unvoiced t is a genuine printed variant of the preceding waredake entry and is not harmonized with it.

runs.text: Por mim meſmo, ou eu. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Wareto is explained as by myself, or I; the pilcrow introduces additional persons or reflexive uses on the next row. The initial gloss remains separate from the continuation's broader list.

runs.text: Por ſi meſmo, ou tu, &c. ou por ſi meſmo.

lines.note: The continuation gives by oneself, thou, and related reflexive uses. Enlarged comparison of both occurrences supports a space in each ſi meſmo; the final OCR ſimeſmo is separated to match that visible gap.
